evidence.source: Shuowen.org, 說文解字 entry for 兒
evidence.text: The Han-period dictionary entry glosses 兒 as “a young child” and explains its seal form as following 儿 and depicting an infant whose cranial fontanel has not yet closed. Duan Yucai’s Qing commentary says the word extended to mean the young or small generally. This records the received historical explanation; it does not independently prove every detail of the depicted anatomy.
evidence.title: 說文解字「兒」

evidence.text: The database records 兒 forms from an oracle-bone inscription (合集20592), bronze inscription (集成06479), Chu manuscripts, and small seal script. It identifies the original meaning as infant and describes the graph as emphasizing the unclosed fontanel. The page labels periods and inscription catalog numbers but does not provide a dated semantic context for the earliest oracle-bone occurrence in the accessible text.
evidence.title: 漢字「兒」：字形演變

evidence.source: Taiwan Ministry of Education, Dictionary of Chinese Character Variants
evidence.text: The dictionary reproduces two Shuowen textual forms: the Great Xu text says 从几, while Duan’s edition reads 从儿; both give the infant/fontanel explanation. Its shape note says the upper 臼-like part represents the infant’s fontanel and the lower part is 儿. It also reports readings ér (child sense) and ní (surname, equivalent to 倪), and notes a Han example in the surname 儿寬. The account confirms historical editorial variation in Shuowen’s component transcription, not a phonetic role for 儿 in the child graph.
evidence.title: [A00277] 兒 - 教育部《異體字字典》

evidence.source: Taiwan Ministry of Education, Dictionary of Chinese Character Variants
evidence.text: The entry cites the child-address use 呼兒 in the Han anonymous poem 飲馬長城窟行; parental address/self-reference and young-man uses are also illustrated with later works, including Li Shangyin’s Tang poem and later historical fiction. It describes the older distinction “兒” for males and “嬰” for females as a dictionary account. Its examples establish attested uses at the cited textual periods, but they do not determine the first occurrence of each semantic extension.
evidence.title: [A00277] 兒 - 教育部《異體字字典》

evidence.text: The text contains 呼兒烹鯉魚 (“call the child to open/cook the carp”), an early literary use of 兒 as a child or household dependent. The page labels it an Eastern Han work but explicitly notes that attribution to Cai Yong is disputed; it lists transmission in 玉臺新詠, 樂府詩集, and 藝文類聚. Thus the wording is preserved in later compilations, and the page’s Eastern Han date is an attribution rather than a securely dated contemporary manuscript.
evidence.title: 飲馬長城窟行 (蔡邕)

evidence.text: Modern Standard Mandarin Pinyin is ér; Guangzhou–Hong Kong Cantonese Jyutping is ji4. The entry reports Middle Chinese fanqie 汝移切 and Baxter’s reconstruction nye, with several scholars’ differing phonetic renderings. It gives Old Chinese Baxter–Sagart 2014 /*ŋe/ and Zhengzhang 2003 /*ŋje/. These are reconstruction-system-specific proposals for the word represented by 兒, not evidence for a sound component inside the pictographic infant graph.
evidence.title: 兒 - Wiktionary, the free dictionary

evidence.text: The entry separately describes 儿 as a standing-person pictogram and radical form of 人, while also identifying contemporary Simplified Chinese 儿 as a simplification of 兒 by omission of 臼. This separation is important: modern simplified 儿 writes the child word through graphic reduction, while historical component/radical 儿 also has an independent person-shaped use. The entry is secondary and its paleographic image sequence was not visually inspected here.
evidence.title: 儿 - Wiktionary, the free dictionary

evidence.text: The page lists Shang oracle-bone and Western Zhou bronze examples and cites the underlying shape collections, but its accessible text does not assign dates or semantic contexts to individual forms. It separately places 兒 in a Zhengzhang-reconstructed phonetic series with characters including 倪, 霓, and 猊; same-series membership concerns sound relations among graphs and does not make 兒 a phonetic component of itself or establish the visual referent of its earliest forms.
evidence.title: 兒 - Wiktionary, the free dictionary

gaps: The Academia Sinica database names Shang oracle-bone and Western Zhou bronze catalog examples, but accessible page text does not give a dated semantic context for the earliest graph use; the images were not visually inspected.

The fontanel interpretation is the standard Shuowen and Sinica account, but the MOE entry notes textual variation in Shuowen component transcription; secondary search results also surfaced a competing topknot/child interpretation. The relevant scholarly discussion and images could not be accessed, so the exact depicted feature remains unresolved.

Earliest attestation of the spoken child word is not established by the retrieved sources. A Han-dynasty poem provides a dated-by-attribution literary example, with authorship disputed and transmission through later compilations.

The semantic paths from child to son, parental address/self-reference, young man, insult, and grammatical suffix are not chronologically established by dictionary gloss order. The sources provide examples but not a full dated semantic history.

The simplification's official promulgation table was not successfully opened; sources inspected establish current relation 儿/兒 and reduction by omission, but the precise formal adoption date was not confirmed here.
No sound component is proposed for the infant pictograph 兒. 儿 has an independent person-shaped radical use, but it is not a phonetic element in 兒's historical formation.
